title: Config-to-exec RCE in official MCP SDKs (June 2026 disclosure wave, CVE-2026-30615/30617/30618/30623/30624/30625/33224/26015/40933)
summary: Anthropic's official MCP SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Java/Rust) pass StdioServerParameters command/args/cwd/env raw to process spawn; any user-controlled config channel (UI field, JSON config, marketplace package, transport-type substitution) becomes arbitrary command execution. Up to 200k estimated vulnerable instances riding 150M+ downloads, 7k+ internet-reachable servers. Anthropic declines to fix ('by design'); mitigation is operator-side: allowlist executables, schema-validate args, strip dangerous env vars (LIBRARY_PATH, NODE_OPTIONS, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS), sandbox child processes. Research first published 2026-04-15 (pre-window), formal disclosure wave 2026-06-16 per Penaxtra.

title: MCP transport-type substitution (SSE/HTTP to STDIO) for command execution (CVE-2026-26015)
summary: An attacker who can POST an MCP server configuration can flip the declared transport from SSE/HTTP to STDIO and append an arbitrary command; the server executes it when the connection is instantiated. STDIO handlers remain enabled internally even where UIs only expose remote transports (DocsGPT, Letta AI). Test for hidden STDIO processing paths behind remote-transport-only interfaces.

title: Zero-click prompt injection to local RCE via IDE MCP config writes (CVE-2026-30615 Windsurf)
summary: Windsurf modified MCP configuration files from web-page content without user consent, chaining page-based prompt injection directly into local command execution. Most IDEs prompt before MCP config modification, but this consent assumption is not universal - verify IDE MCP config handling for consentless writes before relying on the 'user will approve' model.

title: MCP config allowlist bypass via package-runner binaries (npx -c, CVE-2026-30625/40933)
summary: MCP STDIO hardening that allowlists npx (and similar package runners) inherits arbitrary command execution through npx -c/--call, which accepts custom commands and shell scripts. Observed in Upsonic and Flowise. Audit any MCP command allowlist containing a package-runner binary as a bypass primitive.

title: Ecosystem-scale MCP exposure measurement: 43.28% of servers expose destructive-or-execute tools
summary: PolicyLayer classified 517,973 tools across 32,820 working MCP servers (July audit; June audit covered 2,031). 28.1% expose at least one destructive tool (delete/drop/wipe/force-push/cloud removal), 26.2% can execute arbitrary commands, 43.28% expose destructive-or-execute. Stacking: probability a 5-server agent stack exposes such a tool passes 94.1% (99.7% at 10). 'delete' is the most common first token in tool names (9,542). Tool-permission audits are now a baseline requirement for agent deployments.

title: Poisoned MCP tool metadata prevalence and impact (2026 numbers)
summary: Aggregated 2026 stats: 5.5% of public MCP servers carry poisoned tool metadata (Invariant Labs); 84.2% tool-poisoning success with auto-approval enabled (controlled testing); 82% of 2,614 MCP implementations have path-traversal-prone file operations and 34% command-injection-susceptible APIs (Endor Labs); 24,008 secrets found in public MCP configs, 2,117 still valid (GitGuardian). Tool descriptions, system prompts and user messages share one context window at equal trust level - the model cannot distinguish documentation from commands.

title: DNS rebinding against MCP fetch servers over SSE (MCP-S-014)
summary: Classic DNS rebinding ported to MCP: a malicious web page rebinds a domain to 127.0.0.1 between resolution and connection, reaching localhost-bound MCP endpoints over SSE and exfiltrating tool results from the reference fetch MCP server. Confirms 2026 MCP servers inherit web bugs the browser stack solved years ago; validate MCP transport endpoints against rebinding (host-allowlist checks at connect time).

title: CISA guidance: MCP as a trust boundary in AI-driven automation
summary: Government security design guidance (CSI) for AI-driven automation over MCP: treat tool declarations as untrusted input, enforce gateway-level policy, scope credentials, apply least privilege to agent tool access. Authoritative checklist source for coverage mapping of agentic targets.

title: IETF security-considerations draft for MCP (draft-mohiuddin-00)
summary: First IETF-track security considerations document for MCP: threat model for clients/servers, transport security (SSE/HTTP), authorization boundaries, registry/supply-chain trust. Signals formal protocol-level security review; monitor revisions for normative security requirements that may become MCP compliance baselines.

title: MCP spec RC security baseline: gateway-inspectable requests, tighter identity, sandboxed MCP Apps UI
summary: Microsoft's 2026 checkpoint: latest MCP release candidate makes requests carry everything a gateway needs to inspect/enforce per call (no hidden session), tightens client-server identity checks, and adds 'MCP Apps' whose interactive UI the host renders inside a sandbox. Protocol deliberately does not enforce security - re-audit assumptions with each spec revision; 'we reviewed MCP last year' is explicitly stale.

title: MCP-Guard: three-stage defense-in-depth for MCP + MCP-AttackBench benchmark
summary: Peer-reviewed (ACL 2026 Findings) layered MCP defense: lightweight static scanning for overt threats, deep neural detector for semantic attacks (fine-tuned E5-based model reaches 96.01% adversarial-prompt accuracy), then an LLM arbitrator synthesizing signals. Ships MCP-AttackBench, a 70,448-sample GPT-4-augmented benchmark of attack vectors that bypass conventional MCP defenses - usable as a test corpus for agent-LLM workflows.

title: Skill-scanner bypass: truncation via ~100k newline padding (ClawHub/VirusTotal/GPT-5.5)
summary: Trail of Bits bypassed ClawHub's malicious-skill detector (VirusTotal Code Insight + GPT-5.5 guard model) by prepending ~100,000 newlines between benign boilerplate and overtly malicious code: the scanning harness truncates oversized files before reaching the payload, and the VT model became confused. Under an hour to develop. Same file-size-inflation evasion observed in the wild on ClawHub by Unit 42. Never trust a scanner's size-limit handling; test truncation behavior of your own pipeline.

title: Skill-scanner bypass: precompiled .pyc bytecode poisoning (xz-utils pattern in agent skills)
summary: A skill ships benign-looking Python source plus a precompiled utils.cpython-312.pyc that exfiltrates environment variables; Cisco skill-scanner static analyzers did not disassemble the bytecode and LLM analyzers were not steered toward it; skills.sh (Gen/Socket/Snyk) also passed it. Scanner file-type whitelisting and shallow tree traversal leave binary artifacts unevaluated - inspect skill packages for compiled artifacts regardless of visible source.

title: Skill-scanner bypass: archive indirection (.docx/ZIP payload hiding)
summary: SKILL.md instructs the agent to extract real instructions from a .docx file, which is a ZIP archive containing XML plus an embedded malicious shell script (sync1.sh). Pattern-matching scanners treat archives/opaque file types as inert and only follow files explicitly referenced from SKILL.md, so the payload escapes inspection. Move payloads out of file paths scanners prioritize; test whether your scanner recurses into nested archives.

title: LLM-as-judge scanner social engineering: corporate-policy framing defeats semantic analysis
summary: A malicious skill redirecting npm/yarn to an attacker-controlled registry, framed in corporate-compliance language ('AppSec-audited dependency allowlist', 'corporate engineering standards'), was judged safe by Cisco's Claude Sonnet 4.6 scanner (is_safe: true, max_severity LOW) - which worried more about the skill leaking network topology than the registry domain being attacker-controllable. LLM-based risk analysis is vulnerable to persuasion, not just injection; treat scanner verdicts as advisory only.

title: Skill scanners are structurally broken: no scanner reliably detects malicious skills
summary: CSA analysis of ToB's June 3, 2026 findings plus an independent DEV-community study testing classical obfuscation (base85+XOR, affine UTF-8 transforms, multi-stream transposition) against the same scanners: Socket produced no Critical/High alerts even against unobfuscated baselines; Snyk downgraded findings under content splitting; only Gen held Critical/High detection across all conditions. NVIDIA SkillSpector (May 2026, 64 patterns/16 categories, ~87% claimed precision) cannot analyze encrypted/binary code. No single scanner covers all bypass classes - trust model is broken at the root; use curated marketplaces and pin versions.

title: Novel in-the-wild skill threats: runtime agentic affiliate injection and agentic front-running
summary: Unit 42 found five malicious skills that evaded ClawHub's VirusTotal+ClawScan screening (Feb-May 2026): two macOS infostealers with C2 infrastructure, one file-size-inflation evasion skill (independently confirming ToB's truncation finding), and two novel agentic threat classes - runtime agentic affiliate injection (skill injects affiliate/promotional instructions into the agent runtime at execution time) and agentic front-running (skill intercepts/races the agent's own pending actions). Both novel classes are new test dimensions for agent runtime integrity.

title: Behavioral Integrity Verification (BIV): claim-vs-behavior audit for agent skills
summary: Unit 42's BIV compares what a skill claims to do against what it does across metadata, executable code, and natural-language instructions. At registry scale, most skills deviate from declared behavior (mostly sloppy docs) but a dangerous slice carries multi-stage chains where individually benign capabilities combine into credential theft, RCE, or silent exfiltration. Skills stand where mobile apps/browser extensions were a decade ago: require behavioral-integrity checks before install, not after; inventory third-party skills in production agents.

title: MCP servers as unmanaged API sprawl: inventory and policy discipline
summary: Palo Alto Networks frames MCP servers as an unmanaged-API problem: no inventory, no versioning, no access-control discipline across the agent tool surface. Treat MCP endpoints as first-class API assets (discovery, classification, policy). Directly applicable to recon/asset-graph surface mapping for agentic targets.

title: MCP agents as non-human identities: lifecycle governance gap
summary: CYFIRMA threat-intel treatment: each agent is a credentialed principal that authenticates continuously and accumulates permissions across every connected MCP server, with no lifecycle governance, offboarding, or credential rotation in most deployments. A single instruction-channel compromise yields autonomous machine-speed action across every integration in one context window - no file-based or network-layer detection fires. ~9,400 MCP servers in public registries and 150M+ tooling downloads by mid-2026.

title: Microsoft IR: poisoned MCP tool metadata attack pattern in enterprise environments (ASI02/ASI04)
summary: Microsoft Incident Response playbook for the poisoned-MCP-tool-metadata pattern: 'a prompt injection against an agent can trigger an action' - read-write agents shift the impact profile from biased output to performed actions. Maps to OWASP ASI02 Tool Misuse / ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain; IDC projects 28.6M (2025) to 2.2B (2030) active enterprise agents. First-party IR validation that MCP tool poisoning is observed in enterprise environments; includes detection/containment/prevention controls.

title: ShareLock: multi-tool threshold poisoning of MCP servers (Shamir-style secret splitting)
summary: First systematic multi-tool poisoning framework: distributes a malicious instruction across multiple MCP tool descriptions as benign-looking secret shares (Shamir threshold scheme), so no single tool looks malicious and per-tool detectors/manual inspection pass, while the payload activates when the model has read enough fragments. Directly defeats the per-tool scanning assumption behind most 2025-2026 defenses. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2606.)

title: LoginTrap: login-inducing indirect prompt injection against web agents (86% end-to-end success)
summary: Black-box, task-agnostic attack: page-specific indirect injections generated via fuzzing-inspired process make login appear a plausible prerequisite, guiding the agent to an attacker-controlled login page and causing credential/private-data leakage. 86% average end-to-end attack success across LLM backbones; effective across agent architectures and existing defenses. Identifies login inducement as a systematic authentication-boundary risk for LLM-based web agents - test web agents' login flows for inducement.

title: GhostWriter: hidden-payload memory poisoning of tool-using personal agents (~98% injection / ~60% activation)
summary: Two-phase memory attack against long-term memory in tool-using personal agents: injection (adversary sends a hidden attack payload through untrusted content) and activation (poisoned memory retrieved during later tasks). Near-universal injection (~98%) and ~60% average activation against state-of-the-art agents, exploiting the lack of security-focused memory governance. Proposes Agentic Memory Sentry (AMS) defense. Memory poisoning is now demonstrated against production-grade personal agents with tools, not just chat models.

title: MAFIA: query-only memory attacks that survive retrieval competition and input auditing
summary: Extends query-only memory poisoning to realistic settings where 2025 MINJA-style attacks fail: large benign memory pools (retrieval competition) and active input auditing. Placement strategy (memory probing, budget allocation, scheduling) ensures retrieval competitiveness; payloads wrapped in 'compact factual cloaks' preserve malicious effect while passing semantic-similarity audits. Old defenses (semantic filters) are explicitly bypassed. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2608.)

title: FARMA: forged amplifying rationale attacks on agent memory (reasoning-history poisoning)
summary: Forged Amplifying Rationale Memory Attack poisons the agent's stored reasoning history (rationale/chain-of-thought records) rather than facts: forged rationales amplify future decisions toward attacker goals while the agent's evidence trail and auditors see consistent reasoning. Distinct from fact-poisoning (MINJA/MAFIA); targets explainability and audit tooling that reconstruct why actions were taken.

title: PlanFlip: planning-phase prompt injection with cascade amplification in multi-agent systems
summary: Four planning-phase attacks (GoalSubstitution PF-1, PriorityInversion PF-2, ContextPollution PF-3, RoleConfusion PF-4) disguised as plausible tool outputs; a single injection into the Planner's context cascades to corrupt all downstream sub-tasks. Across 9 frontier LLMs / 3,479 episodes: GPT-5 has highest ASR (0.68) - capability amplifies vulnerability; homogeneous pipelines show a correlated-agent blind spot where same-backbone Critics report alignment while plans are restructured (-0.20 to -0.32 semantic deviation, r=0.943). Test planners as single points of failure; vary backbone diversity in multi-agent pipelines. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2607.)

title: CLI command-composition risk (CCR) in LLM coding agents (MOSAIC)
summary: New exploit surface: individually benign CLI commands form dangerous producer-consumer state relations across a command trace - one command writes OS state a later command reads - even when no single command contains malicious text. Instruction-layer attacks and defenses miss this; systematic knowledge-guided command enumeration (MOSAIC) replaces naive generation. Test coding agents for stateful command sequences, not just single-command injection. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2607.)

title: PI-Hunter: automated red-teaming that localizes prompt injections
summary: Google Cloud AI Research: existing red-teaming optimizes attack success only; PI-Hunter also localizes where the injection landed (tool description vs memory vs retrieved content) so fixes target the actual vulnerable component. Useful as the template for injection-triage workflows in agent targets. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2606.)

title: Adversarial output propagation as trusted input in multi-agent pipelines
summary: Multi-agent LLM pipelines introduce a security gap absent in single-agent settings: once an agent accepts adversarial content, it is propagated as trusted input throughout the pipeline - intermediate agent outputs are a new injection channel. Structural, architecture-level vulnerability; test inter-agent handoffs for sanitization and trust marking. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2608.)

title: Hybrid static+dynamic analysis for secure MCP tool use
summary: Prior MCP tool-use defenses rely on static analysis (inspecting prompts/generations); this work combines static inspection with dynamic behavior verification of MCP tool invocations, positioning runtime checking as the missing half of MCP defenses. Aligns with Unit 42's behavioral-integrity approach; dynamic verification is the 2026 direction for MCP tool-use protection. (Month-level date from arXiv ID 2607.)

title: PortSwigger: Burp AT agentic security testing + trusted AI testing framing
summary: PortSwigger launched Burp AT, an AI-driven assistant embedded in Burp Suite (2026-07-27), followed by 'From capable AI models to trusted security testing' (2026-07-30) framing verification, traceability and containment as the requirements for trusting AI in security testing. Product signal that 2026 testing workflows are moving to agent-assisted operation; also defines the trust bar AI-assisted findings must meet before they are treated as evidence.

title: HTTP Terminator: AI agent independently discovering novel HTTP attack techniques
summary: James Kettle / PortSwigger Research (2026-08-05; blog companion 2026-08-12): an AI agent (HTTP Terminator) independently discovered and weaponized new HTTP-level attack techniques rather than regurgitating known CVEs. Bleeding-edge on two axes: (a) capability signal for what autonomous agents can do against web targets, and (b) methodology for verifying agent-discovered findings - directly relevant to impact-verifier rigor for AI-generated findings.
